topic: Eligibility and conditions for taking ITC
question: As per Section 16(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, a registered person is entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him subject to certain conditions. Which of the following is a fundamental condition regarding the use of such goods or services for claiming Input Tax Credit (ITC)?
option_A: The registered person must have actually paid the tax charged on the supply to the supplier before claiming the credit.
option_B: The goods or services or both must be used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business.
option_C: The goods or services or both must be used or intended to be used for personal consumption of the registered person.
option_D: The goods or services or both must be used or intended to be used exclusively for the manufacture of capital goods.
explanation: Section 16(1) states that every registered person shall be entitled to take credit of input tax charged on any supply of goods or services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business. If goods are diverted for non-business purposes, the registered person is not entitled to ITC on such goods.
option_explanations: {"A": "This incorrectly conflates the condition of possession of invoice and receipt of goods with payment of tax to the supplier. Under Section 16(2), the conditions relate to possession of invoice, receipt of goods, and the supplier having furnished the return. Payment to the supplier is not a statutory condition for ITC eligibility under Section 16.", "B": "Section 16(1) explicitly mandates that ITC is available only on goods or services which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of the business. This establishes the direct nexus between the input and business activity required for credit eligibility.", "C": "This is the direct opposite of the requirement under Section 16(1). The statute explicitly requires goods/services to be used 'in the course or furtherance of his business'. Use for personal consumption is a non-business purpose, and Section 17(5) specifically blocks ITC on goods/services used for personal consumption.", "D": "This incorrectly narrows the scope of ITC eligibility. Section 16(1) permits ITC for goods/services used 'in the course or furtherance of his business', which is a broad requirement covering all business activities including trading, services, and manufacturing. The statute does not require exclusive use for manufacture of capital goods."}

question: Mr. A, a registered person, is in possession of a tax invoice for a supply of goods. However, the details of the said invoice have not been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies. Can Mr. A avail the Input Tax Credit (ITC) on the basis of the tax invoice in his possession?
option_A: Yes, because possession of a valid tax invoice is the primary condition for availing Input Tax Credit under Section 16(2)(a).
option_B: Yes, because the recipient can claim ITC based on the invoice if the tax has been charged and the goods have been received.
option_C: No, because the recipient has not actually paid the tax amount to the supplier against the said invoice.
option_D: No, because the details of the invoice have not been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and communicated to the recipient.
explanation: As per Section 16(2), a registered person is not entitled to credit of any input tax unless the details of the invoice have been furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and such details have been communicated to the recipient in the manner specified under section 37. This condition is in addition to possessing a valid tax invoice under Section 16(2)(a).
option_explanations: {"A": "This incorrectly assumes that satisfying one condition (possession of invoice under Section 16(2)(a)) is sufficient. Section 16(2) uses 'and' to connect the conditions; the invoice details must also be furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies under Section 16(2)(aa).", "B": "This overlooks the mandatory requirement introduced by Section 16(2)(aa). Even if goods are received and tax is charged, ITC cannot be availed unless the supplier has furnished the invoice details in the statement of outward supplies and these have been communicated to the recipient.", "C": "This gives the right answer (No) but for the wrong reason. Payment of tax to the supplier is not a condition for ITC under Section 16. The correct reason for denial is the failure to satisfy Section 16(2)(aa) regarding furnishing of invoice details in the statement of outward supplies.", "D": "Section 16(2)(aa) mandates that the details of the invoice or debit note must be furnished by the supplier in the statement of outward supplies and communicated to the recipient. Mere possession of the tax invoice is insufficient if this condition is not met."}

question: M/s Alpha Ltd., a manufacturing company, availed works contract services for renovation of its factory building. The expenditure for such renovation was not capitalized in the books of account but was treated as revenue expenditure in accordance with the applicable Accounting Standards. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the admissibility of Input Tax Credit (ITC) on the GST paid for such works contract services?
option_A: ITC is blocked because the factory building is an immovable property other than plant and machinery.
option_B: ITC is allowed since the renovation expenditure is not capitalized in the books of account.
option_C: ITC is blocked because renovation of a factory building amounts to construction of an immovable property other than plant and machinery.
option_D: ITC is allowed only if M/s Alpha Ltd. is in the business of providing works contract services to others.
explanation: Section 17(5)(c) blocks ITC on works contract services supplied for construction of an immovable property, other than plant and machinery. The term 'construction' explicitly includes re-construction, renovation, additions or alterations, or repairs, but only 'to the extent of capitalization' to the said immovable property. The reference material states that if renovation or repairs are not capitalized, it would not tantamount to construction under GST law. Consequently, ITC on works contract services availed for such construction (which is not capitalized) is allowed to all recipients irrespective of their line of business. Since Alpha Ltd. did not capitalize the expenditure, the blocking provision does not apply.
option_explanations: {"A": "While the factory building is indeed an immovable property other than plant and machinery, the candidate fails to apply the specific exception for non-capitalized renovation/repairs. The blocking of ITC under Section 17(5)(c) applies only when the construction (including renovation) is capitalized.", "B": "As per the definition of 'construction' in the context of blocked credits, renovation amounts to construction only if it is capitalized. Since the expense is treated as revenue expenditure (not capitalized), it does not fall within the blocked credit provisions of section 17(5)(c).", "C": "This option incorrectly applies the blocking provision by ignoring the vital qualification regarding capitalization. The definition of 'construction' explicitly includes renovation only 'to the extent of capitalization'. Since the facts state the expenditure was not capitalized, it does not amount to 'construction' for the purpose of Section 17(5)(c), and thus ITC is not blocked.", "D": "This incorrectly applies the restriction for works contract services used for further supply of works contract services (sub-contracting). The reference material clarifies that when renovation/repairs are not capitalized, ITC is allowed to 'all the recipients irrespective of their line of business'."}

question: M/s Beta Pvt. Ltd., a textile manufacturer, availed outdoor catering services for running a canteen in its factory premises for the benefit of its employees. The setting up of the canteen is required under the Factories Act, 1948. The company seeks to claim Input Tax Credit (ITC) on the GST paid for these outdoor catering services. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the admissibility of such ITC?
option_A: ITC is blocked because the outdoor catering service is provided for the personal consumption of employees.
option_B: ITC is allowed since the outdoor catering service is obligatory for the employer to provide under the Factories Act, 1948.
option_C: ITC is allowed only if the outdoor catering service is used for making an outward taxable supply of the same category of services.
option_D: ITC is blocked since outdoor catering services are explicitly mentioned in the blocked credits list under Section 17(5)(b).
explanation: Section 17(5)(b)(i) read with Section 17(5)(b)(iii) blocks ITC on food and beverages, outdoor catering, etc. However, the proviso to section 17(5)(b) states that ITC shall be available where it is obligatory for an employer to provide such goods or services to its employees under any law for the time being in force. The reference material explicitly clarifies via Circular No. 172/04/2022 that this proviso applies to the whole of section 17(5)(b) and provides the specific example that where a company sets up a canteen in its factory under the Factories Act, 1948, ITC on such outdoor catering is allowed.
option_explanations: {"A": "While outdoor catering for employees typically constitutes blocked credit as personal consumption, the candidate fails to recognize that the statutory obligation exception overrides this general principle. The Factories Act, 1948 mandate triggers the proviso, making the ITC admissible.", "B": "While outdoor catering is generally a blocked credit under section 17(5)(b)(i), the proviso to section 17(5)(b) creates an exception where the inward supply is obligatory for an employer to provide to its employees under any law. Since the canteen is mandated by the Factories Act, 1948, the ITC is admissible.", "C": "The candidate confuses the first proviso (same category supply) with the second proviso (statutory obligation). The first proviso applies to general cases, whereas the second proviso specifically allows ITC where the employer is obligated under law to provide such services, regardless of outward supply.", "D": "The candidate ignores the proviso to Section 17(5)(b) which creates an exception for goods/services obligatory under law. The reference material confirms via Circular No. 172/04/2022 that this proviso applies to the entire Section 17(5)(b), allowing ITC in this specific statutory scenario."}

question: Alpha Ltd., a registered person, purchased a machine from Beta Machinery Ltd. for ₹10,00,000 plus GST. The machine was delivered under Invoice No. 101 dated 15th February 2026. Subsequently, Beta Machinery Ltd. performed installation and calibration, raising Debit Note No. DN/05 dated 10th April 2026 for ₹1,00,000 plus GST. Alpha Ltd. filed its annual return for FY 2025-26 on 31st December 2026. Determine the last date by which Alpha Ltd. can avail Input Tax Credit (ITC) on the tax paid on Debit Note No. DN/05.
explanation: According to Section 16(4) of the CGST Act, ITC on invoices or debit notes pertaining to a financial year can be availed until the 30th of November of the succeeding financial year or the date of filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. The Study Material clarifies that in the case of debit notes, the date of issuance of the debit note is relevant to determine the 'pertaining' financial year, not the date of the underlying invoice. Here, the debit note was issued on 10th April 2026, which falls in Financial Year 2026-27. Therefore, the time limit is calculated with reference to FY 2026-27. The deadline is the earlier of the date of filing the annual return for FY 2026-27 or 30th November 2027. Consequently, the last date to avail ITC on the debit note is 30th November 2027. The filing of the annual return for FY 2025-26 on 31st December 2026 is irrelevant for the debit note's time limit.
option_explanations: {"A": "Since the debit note was issued in April 2026 (FY 2026-27), the relevant financial year for determining the time limit under Section 16(4) is FY 2026-27. The deadline is the earlier of the date of filing the annual return for FY 2026-27 or 30th November 2027. Thus, the outer limit is 30th November 2027.", "B": "This incorrectly applies the deadline for the invoice's financial year (FY 2025-26) by using the annual return filing date mentioned in the facts, rather than calculating the deadline based on the financial year in which the debit note was issued (FY 2026-27).", "C": "This incorrectly calculates the deadline as one year from the date of issuance of the debit note, misapplying the general time limit concept rather than using the statutory cutoff of 30th November of the succeeding financial year.", "D": "This incorrectly links the debit note to the financial year of the underlying invoice (FY 2025-26), rather than using the date of issuance of the debit note (April 2026) to determine the relevant financial year for the time limit."}

question: Delta Traders, a registered person, had its registration cancelled with effect from 1st August 2025. The cancellation order was subsequently revoked on 20th October 2026. Delta Traders filed all pending returns for the period from the cancellation date to the revocation date on 15th November 2026 (within 30 days of revocation). Delta Traders possesses an invoice dated 1st May 2025 (pertaining to FY 2025-26) for which ITC was not availed before cancellation. Determine the last date for Delta Traders to avail ITC on the invoice dated 1st May 2025.
explanation: Section 16(6) provides a specific relaxation for cases where registration is cancelled and subsequently revoked. If the taxpayer files the returns for the period from cancellation to revocation within 30 days of the revocation order, the time limit to avail ITC under Section 16(4) is extended to the date of filing of those returns. However, this extension is subject to the condition that the time limit under Section 16(4) had not already expired on the date of cancellation. In this scenario, the invoice is dated 1st May 2025. The normal deadline under Section 16(4) would be 30th November 2026. The registration was cancelled on 1st August 2025. On the date of cancellation, the Section 16(4) deadline (30th November 2026) had not expired. Therefore, the relaxation applies. Since the returns were filed on 15th November 2026, this becomes the last date to avail the ITC.
option_explanations: {"A": "This applies the standard Section 16(4) time limit without considering the specific relaxation under Section 16(6), which extends the deadline to the date of filing returns when registration is cancelled and revoked under the prescribed conditions.", "B": "This incorrectly uses the effective date of cancellation of registration as the cutoff for availing ITC, ignoring the proviso to Section 16(6) which extends the time limit if the original Section 16(4) deadline had not expired on the date of cancellation.", "C": "This incorrectly calculates the deadline as 30 days from the revocation order date (20th October 2026), confusing the time limit for filing returns with the actual extended deadline for availing ITC.", "D": "Section 16(6) provides a relaxation for revoked registrations. If returns are filed within 30 days of revocation, the time limit to avail ITC is extended to the date of filing those returns, provided the original Section 16(4) time limit had not expired on the date of cancellation."}

question: Which of the following statements regarding the methodology for determination of input tax credit on capital goods under Rule 43 are correct? (select all that apply)
option_A: The useful life of capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies shall be taken as five years from the date of the invoice for such goods.
option_B: The amount of input tax on capital goods used exclusively for effecting taxable supplies including zero-rated supplies shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger.
option_C: The amount of input tax on capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies shall not be credited to the electronic credit ledger.
option_D: The useful life of capital goods used for both taxable and exempt supplies is taken as five years from the date of the invoice for such goods.
explanation: Rule 43 prescribes the manner of determining ITC on capital goods. It mandates that credit for capital goods used exclusively for non-business or exempt purposes is blocked. For capital goods used exclusively for taxable supplies, full credit is allowed. For common capital goods (used for both taxable and exempt supplies), the credit is credited to the ledger and the useful life is deemed to be five years for the purpose of reversal calculations.
option_explanations: {"A": "The five-year useful life rule applies only to common capital goods used for both taxable and exempt supplies (covered under clause (c) of Rule 43). For capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies, the credit itself is not allowed to be credited to the electronic credit ledger, so the question of useful life for reversal does not arise.", "B": "Rule 43(1)(b) provides that input tax on capital goods used exclusively for taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) shall be credited to the electronic credit ledger.", "C": "Rule 43(1)(a) specifies that input tax on capital goods used exclusively for non-business purposes or exempt supplies shall not be credited to the electronic credit ledger.", "D": "Rule 43(1)(c) explicitly states that the useful life of capital goods (not covered under exclusive use) shall be taken as five years from the date of the invoice."}

question: Which of the following situations require the apportionment of input tax credit under section 17 of the CGST Act, 2017? (select all that apply)
option_A: When goods and/or services are used by the registered person partly for the purpose of business and partly for other purposes.
option_B: When goods and/or services are used by the registered person exclusively for making taxable supplies including zero-rated supplies.
option_C: When goods and/or services are used by the registered person partly for making taxable supplies including zero-rated supplies and partly for making exempt supplies.
option_D: When goods and/or services are used by the registered person exclusively for non-business purposes.
explanation: The study material explicitly lists the situations requiring apportionment of credit. These are: (a) partly for business and partly for other purposes [Section 17(1)], and (b) partly for taxable supplies and partly for exempt supplies [Section 17(2)]. In these cases, only the proportionate ITC attributable to the business purpose or taxable supply is available.
option_explanations: {"A": "Section 17(1) read with the study material specifies that apportionment is required when goods/services are used partly for business and partly for other purposes.", "B": "Apportionment is required only when there is a mix of uses (partly business/partly other, or partly taxable/partly exempt). When goods/services are used exclusively for taxable supplies including zero-rated supplies, full credit is available without any apportionment.", "C": "Section 17(2) read with the study material specifies that apportionment is required when goods/services are used partly for taxable supplies and partly for exempt supplies.", "D": "Apportionment applies when goods/services are used partly for business and partly for other purposes. When goods/services are used exclusively for non-business purposes, no credit is available at all - there is nothing to apportion."}

question: Satyamev Printers undertakes the printing of books where the content is supplied by the publisher, but the physical inputs including paper belong to the printer. The supply is billed at a single price. What is the nature and tax treatment of this supply?
option_A: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of goods, being the principal supply.
option_B: It is a mixed supply and shall be treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax.
option_C: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of goods since the printed books are physically delivered to the publisher.
option_D: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of services, being the principal supply.
explanation: The supply described is a composite supply because it comprises two or more supplies (printing service and goods like paper) naturally bundled in conjunction with each other. According to the analysis in the material, for the printing of books where physical inputs belong to the printer, the principal supply is the supply of printing services. Under Section 8(a), a composite supply is treated as a supply of its principal supply. Therefore, the transaction is treated as a supply of services chargeable to the rate applicable to printing services.
option_explanations: {"A": "While the candidate correctly identifies the transaction as a composite supply, they misidentify the principal supply. The material clarifies that when physical inputs belong to the printer, the supply of printing is the principal supply (a service), not the goods.", "B": "The candidate confuses composite supply with mixed supply. Printing of books with physical inputs from the printer is naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business, making it a composite supply, not a mixed supply.", "C": "The candidate focuses on the physical delivery of goods (books) rather than the statutory condition that determines the principal supply. The material specifies that where physical inputs belong to the printer, printing is the principal supply (service).", "D": "As per the reference material, the supply of printed books where physical inputs belong to the printer is a composite supply. The principal supply is the supply of printing services, and thus the entire supply is treated as a supply of services."}

subject: IDT
question: A taxable person supplies a gift pack comprising chocolates, candies, sweets, and balloons for a single price. These items can be supplied independently but are sold together. What is the tax liability applicable to this supply?
option_A: It is a mixed supply and shall be treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the highest rate of tax.
option_B: It is a mixed supply and each item in the gift pack shall be taxed separately at the rate applicable to each item.
option_C: It is a composite supply and shall be treated as a supply of its principal supply.
option_D: It is a mixed supply and shall be treated as a supply of that particular supply which attracts the lowest rate of tax.
explanation: The supply is a mixed supply because the individual items (chocolates, candies, sweets, balloons) are not naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business and are independent of each other. Under Section 2(74), a mixed supply involves two or more individual supplies made in conjunction with each other for a single price which does not constitute a composite supply. As per Section 8(b), a mixed supply is treated as a supply of that particular supply that attracts the highest rate of tax.
option_explanations: {"A": "The items (chocolates, candies, etc.) are not naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business and are independent supplies. Since they are supplied together for a single price but do not constitute a composite supply, they form a mixed supply, which attracts the highest rate of tax among the components.", "B": "The candidate misunderstands the tax treatment of mixed supply. When multiple items are supplied together for a single price and constitute a mixed supply, they are not taxed separately but are treated as a single supply attracting the highest rate of tax.", "C": "The candidate confuses mixed supply with composite supply. The items (chocolates, candies, sweets, balloons) are not naturally bundled in the ordinary course of business and can be supplied independently, making it a mixed supply.", "D": "The candidate correctly identifies the supply as mixed supply but incorrectly applies the tax treatment. Section 8(b) mandates that a mixed supply is treated as a supply that attracts the highest rate of tax, not the lowest."}

topic: Activities treated as supply without consideration
question: Mr. Chakmak, a proprietor registered in Delhi, received architectural services without consideration from his son located in the US. Which of the following statements correctly determines the taxability of this transaction under the GST law?
option_A: It will not qualify as supply in either case, since services received without consideration from a related person can never be treated as supply under the GST law.
option_B: It will qualify as supply in both cases, since import of services by a related person without consideration is treated as supply irrespective of whether it is in the course or furtherance of business.
option_C: It will not qualify as supply if the services are received with respect to his newly constructed house, but will qualify as supply if received with respect to his office in Delhi.
option_D: It will not qualify as supply in either case, since the services received by way of gift from his son (a related person) are exempt up to ₹50,000 in value in a financial year.
explanation: The transaction involves the import of services without consideration from a related person (son). Under section 7(1)(c) read with Entry 4 of Schedule I, import of services by a person from a related person or from any of his other establishments outside India, in the course or furtherance of business, is treated as supply even without consideration. The reference material explicitly distinguishes between personal and business use: if the architectural services are for a newly constructed house (personal purpose), it is not in the course or furtherance of business and thus not a supply. However, if the services are for his office in Delhi, they are in the course of business and constitute a supply. The exception for gifts up to ₹50,000 applies to employer-employee relationships (Entry 2 of Schedule I) and is not relevant to a father-son transaction involving import of services.
option_explanations: {"A": "This incorrectly assumes that absence of consideration automatically exempts the transaction. Under Entry 4 of Schedule I, import of services without consideration from a related person IS treated as supply if received in the course or furtherance of business.", "B": "This confuses the rule for import of services WITH consideration (which is supply regardless of business purpose) with import WITHOUT consideration (which requires the 'in course or furtherance of business' condition).", "C": "As per the provisions of Schedule I read with section 7(1)(c), import of services by a person from a related person without consideration is treated as supply only if it is in the course or furtherance of business. Services for a personal house are not in the course of business, whereas services for an office are.", "D": "The gift exemption up to ₹50,000 applies only to employer-employee relationships under the proviso to section 7(1)(c), not to father-son transactions involving import of services."}

question: Alpha Ltd. (principal) appointed Beta Ltd. (agent) to procure raw materials. Beta Ltd. receives the raw materials on behalf of Alpha Ltd. and issues the invoice in its own name. In a separate transaction, Alpha Ltd. permanently disposed of business assets on which Input Tax Credit (ITC) was availed, without receiving any consideration. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the taxability of these transactions?
option_A: The transaction between Alpha Ltd. and Beta Ltd. is not treated as supply since Beta Ltd. received the raw materials rather than supplied them, and the disposal of business assets by Alpha Ltd. is treated as supply only if ITC was availed on such assets.
option_B: Neither transaction qualifies as supply since both are made without consideration, and the GST law requires consideration for a transaction to be treated as supply.
option_C: The transaction between Alpha Ltd. and Beta Ltd. is treated as supply of goods by the principal to the agent, and the disposal of business assets by Alpha Ltd. is not treated as supply since it is without consideration.
option_D: The transaction between Alpha Ltd. and Beta Ltd. is treated as supply of goods by the agent to the principal, and the disposal of business assets by Alpha Ltd. is treated as supply even without consideration.
explanation: The question tests two distinct provisions of Schedule I. First, regarding the principal-agent relationship: Para 3(b) of Schedule I states that supply of goods by an agent to his principal where the agent undertakes to receive such goods on behalf of the principal is treated as supply even without consideration. Since Beta Ltd. received goods on behalf of Alpha Ltd., this constitutes a supply. Second, regarding the disposal of assets: Para 1 of Schedule I deems the permanent transfer or disposal of business assets as supply if ITC was availed on such assets, even without consideration. The reference material confirms that permanent transfer/disposal of business assets where ITC is availed is a 'Deemed Supply'.
option_explanations: {"A": "The first part incorrectly applies the rule: Para 3 of Schedule I specifically covers supply by an agent to principal where the agent undertakes to receive goods on behalf of the principal. The second part correctly states the ITC condition but the overall option is incorrect because the principal-agent transaction IS a supply.", "B": "This ignores Schedule I which specifically deems certain activities as supply even without consideration, including principal-agent transactions (Para 3) and permanent disposal of business assets where ITC was availed (Para 1).", "C": "First, the agent received goods on behalf of the principal, so the supply is from agent to principal (not principal to agent). Second, permanent disposal of business assets on which ITC was availed is deemed supply under Para 1 of Schedule I even without consideration.", "D": "Under Para 3 of Schedule I, supply of goods by an agent to a principal where the agent undertakes to receive such goods on behalf of the principal is treated as supply without consideration. Separately, under Para 1 of Schedule I, permanent transfer/disposal of business assets where ITC was availed is deemed supply."}

question: Which of the following statements correctly state the time of supply of goods under section 12 of the CGST Act, 2017? (select all that apply)
option_A: The time of supply of goods is the earlier of the date of issue of invoice (or last date for issue of invoice) or the date of receipt of payment.
option_B: The time of supply of goods is the earlier of the date of actual supply of goods or the date of issue of invoice.
option_C: Where the supplier receives an amount up to one thousand rupees in excess of the amount indicated in the tax invoice, the time of supply to the extent of such excess is, at the option of the supplier, the date of issue of invoice.
option_D: The date on which the supplier receives the payment is the date on which the payment is entered in his books of account or the date on which the payment is credited to his bank account, whichever is earlier.
explanation: Section 12(2) establishes the general rule for the time of supply of goods as the earlier of the invoice date (or due date) or the payment date. Explanation 2 defines the payment date for this purpose. Additionally, the proviso to Section 12(2) provides a specific relaxation for small excess payments (up to ₹1,000), allowing the supplier to opt for the invoice date as the time of supply for such excess.
option_explanations: {"A": "Section 12(2) explicitly provides that the time of supply of goods shall be the earlier of the date of issue of invoice (or the last date for issue of invoice) or the date on which the supplier receives the payment.", "B": "Under Section 12(2), the time of supply of goods is the earlier of the invoice date or the payment date, not the date of actual supply. The date of actual supply is relevant for change in rate of tax provisions under Section 14, not for determining the general time of supply.", "C": "The proviso to Section 12(2) grants the supplier an option to treat the date of issue of invoice as the time of supply for excess amounts received up to one thousand rupees.", "D": "Explanation 2 to Section 12(2) clarifies that the date of receipt of payment is determined as the date of entry in the books of account or the date of credit to the bank account, whichever is earlier."}

question: Which of the following dates are considered in determining the time of supply of goods under reverse charge mechanism? (select all that apply)
option_A: Date on which goods are received.
option_B: Date on which the payment is recorded in the books of account of the recipient of goods.
option_C: Date on which the payment is debited from the bank account of the recipient of goods.
option_D: Date on which the payment is credited to the bank account of the supplier of goods.
explanation: For goods taxable under reverse charge, the time of supply is the earliest of: (1) date of receipt of goods, (2) date on which payment is recorded in the books of account of the recipient, (3) date on which payment is debited from the bank account of the recipient, or (4) the 31st day from the issue of invoice. Options A, B, and C correctly state three of the four dates considered in this determination. Option D is incorrect as it refers to the supplier's bank account, which is relevant for forward charge, not reverse charge.

The relevant dates are when payment is recorded in the recipient's books or debited from the recipient's bank account, not when it is credited to the supplier's account."}

topic: Place of supply of services domestic
question: M/s Sunrise Logistics Pvt. Ltd., a registered person located in Mumbai, Maharashtra, provides services of transportation of goods (via road) to M/s Global Traders. The goods are transported from Delhi to Chennai. M/s Global Traders is an unregistered person, and its billing address as per the records of M/s Sunrise Logistics is in Jaipur, Rajasthan. However, M/s Global Traders has no presence or business operations in Rajasthan, and the services are effectively used by its branch office in Chennai, Tamil Nadu. Determine the place of supply of the transportation services.
explanation:
The place of supply of services where both the supplier and recipient are in India is governed by Section 12 of the IGST Act. Section 12 does not contain a specific provision for the transportation of goods (unlike Section 12(8) for passenger transport or specific clauses for other services). Therefore, the default provision under Section 12(2) applies. 

Section 12(2)(b) provides that for services made to an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location of the recipient where the address on record exists, and the location of the supplier in other cases. The Study Material explicitly states that for unregistered persons, the place of supply is the location of such unregistered person if the address is available in the records of the supplier. The fact that the service is effectively used in Chennai or that the goods moved from Delhi to Chennai is irrelevant for the default rule. The statutory requirement is satisfied by the 'address on record', which is Jaipur. The Study Material emphasizes that the provisions of Section 12 are in relation to domestic supply and the default rule relies on the address available in the records.
option_explanations: {"A": "The candidate may incorrectly apply the concept of 'place of effective use and enjoyment' (which is a specific exception under Section 13(13) for cross-border supplies or specific notifications) to this domestic transaction. Under Section 12, for unregistered persons, the statutory place of supply is determined by the address on record, not where the service is effectively used.", "B": "Under Section 12(2)(b)(i) of the IGST Act, for services provided to an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location of the recipient where the address on record exists. Since the address of M/s Global Traders on record is in Jaipur, Rajasthan, that is the place of supply, regardless of where the goods are transported or where the service is effectively used.", "C": "The candidate may misapply the default provision under Section 12(2)(b) by concluding that since the recipient is unregistered, the 'other cases' clause (location of supplier) applies. However, the 'other cases' clause only applies when the address on record does *not* exist; here, the billing address in Jaipur exists in the supplier's records, so the location of the recipient (Jaipur) is the correct place of supply.", "D": "The candidate may incorrectly rely on the origin and destination of the goods transported (Delhi to Chennai) to determine the place of supply. However, for transportation of goods services where both supplier and recipient are in India, there is no specific provision in Section 12 linking the place of supply to the location of goods, so the default rule based on the recipient's address on record applies instead."}

question: M/s Eventz India, a registered entity in New Delhi, is engaged by M/s Tech Solutions, an unregistered person located in Gurugram, Haryana, to organize a 3-day business conference. The conference is scheduled to be held in Kathmandu, Nepal. M/s Eventz India raises the invoice for their services on 10th October, 2026. Determine the place of supply of the event organization services provided by M/s Eventz India.
explanation: The place of supply for event management services is determined by the specific provision under Section 12(7) of the IGST Act, not the default provision. Section 12(7) distinguishes between registered and unregistered recipients. For an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location where the event is actually held. However, the Study Material clarifies the exception: 'if the event is held outside India, the place of supply is the location of recipient.' Since the facts state the event is in Kathmandu (outside India), the exception applies, shifting the place of supply to the location of the recipient, which is Gurugram, Haryana.
option_explanations: {"A": "The candidate may correctly recall the general rule that for event management services provided to an unregistered person, the place of supply is where the event is actually held, but fail to register the crucial exception stated in the proviso: if the event is held outside India, the place of supply shifts to the location of the recipient.", "B": "As per Section 12(7)(a)(ii) of the IGST Act, for event organization services provided to an unregistered person, the place of supply is the location where the event is actually held. However, a proviso states that if the event is held outside India, the place of supply shall be the location of the recipient. Since the event is in Kathmandu (outside India) and the recipient is in Gurugram, the place of supply is Gurugram.", "C": "The candidate may ignore the specific provision for event management services (Section 12(7)) and apply the default provision (Section 12(2)) for unregistered persons incorrectly. Under the default rule for unregistered persons without an address on record, the place of supply would be the supplier's location (New Delhi), but this ignores the specific event management provision.", "D": "The candidate may confuse the facts of the current question with the illustration provided in the Study Material (where Mr. Murthy's event was held in Bengaluru). This represents a failure to apply the legal provision to the specific facts of the case at hand, instead recalling the answer to a different illustrative example."}

topic: Eligibility and conditions for taking ITC
question: PQR Ltd., a registered supplier, provided a post supply discount to a customer in October 2026 pursuant to an agreement entered into in September 2026 (after the original supply). The supplier issued a credit note. Assuming the amendment proposed by the Finance Act, 2026 has come into effect, which of the following statements is valid regarding the treatment of Input Tax Credit (ITC) by the recipient?
option_A: The recipient is required to reverse the proportionate ITC as the discount will be excluded from the value of supply upon issuance of credit note.
option_B: The recipient is not required to reverse the input tax credit as there is no reduction in the original transaction value of the supply when a credit note is issued.
option_C: The recipient is eligible to retain the ITC as the discount provided is in the nature of a post supply discount which does not affect the tax liability of the original transaction.
option_D: The recipient cannot claim any reduction in value of supply as the post supply discount agreement was not in existence at the time of the original supply and cannot be linked invoice-wise.
explanation: The Finance Act, 2026 proposes to amend the conditions for availing post supply discount. As per the reference material, when the amendment comes into effect, it will no longer be necessary for the post supply discount to be in terms of an agreement existing at the time of supply and capable of being linked invoice-wise. The discount will be excluded from the value of supply if the supplier issues a credit note and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. Since the question assumes the amendment has come into effect, the recipient must reverse the proportionate ITC.
option_explanations: {"A": "Under the amendment proposed by the Finance Act, 2026, once it comes into effect, the discount will be excluded from the value of supply if the supplier issues a credit note and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. The requirement for the agreement to exist at the time of supply is removed.", "B": "This statement reflects the position under the earlier clarification where ITC reversal was not required for financial/commercial credit notes since there was no reduction in the original transaction value. However, under the amended provisions, the discount will be excluded from the value of supply only if the recipient reverses the proportionate ITC.", "C": "This incorrectly assumes that post supply discounts continue to have no impact on ITC retention. Under the Finance Act, 2026 amendment, the statutory mechanism explicitly requires ITC reversal for the discount to be validly excluded from the value of supply, making it mandatory for the recipient to reverse proportionate ITC.", "D": "This statement applies the pre-amendment conditions which required the agreement to exist at the time of supply and be capable of being linked invoice-wise. The Finance Act, 2026 amendment specifically removes these conditions, making it unnecessary for the agreement to exist at the time of supply."}
